text.p: Rem Vyakhirev, chairman of Russian gas monopoly Gazprom, outlined his top five priorities for the company on Monday.

Vyakhirev, speaking at a conference organised by the Royal Institute of International Affairs, said Gazprom's priorities are: to reconstruct existing but deteriorating gas installations; rebuild the internal distribution system; rebuild the country's export lines; press ahead with the construction of gas-fired power stations; and develop new technology for modernising the industry.
Gas demand in Russia is expected to grow from this year as the economic crisis seen since the collapse of the Soviet Union bottoms out.
"We expect a rise in consumption of three to four billion cubic metres (bcm) this year. By 2005, consumption will increase to 1991 levels, and it will then grow to 2010," Vyakhirev said.
Exports are also set to grow, he said.
Between 1994 and 1995, exports to countries other than CIS states and the Baltic republics grew by 11.5 bcm to 117.4 bcm, while exports to CIS republics and the Baltics reached 73.2 bcm last year.

He added that last year 18.7 percent of West European gas demand was met from Russia, "but to develop this further Gazprom must increase output by not less than 50 bcm a year. This is not expansionism, this is just to keep our market share".

Russia is developing several new export routes, he said. Gas from the giant Yamal peninsula, which will eventually be transported on a new pipeline through Belarus and Poland to Germany, will start production after 2000, peak at 200-250 bcm a year, and will enable Russia to supply Europe well into the next century.

Vyakhirev also confirmed Gazprom will "definitely" go ahead with a 370 km submarine line under the Black Sea to supply Turkey. "This will involve a pipe with a wall thickness of 34 cm and a depth of 2,100 metres, a world first", he said.
Deliveries to the Balkans and Turkey are set to increase from 19.5 bcm in 1995 to 58 bcm by 2010.
And a north European project, taking gas through Finland and Sweden to Denmark by land and sea, is under consideration. "If a study shows it is viable, it will be built," he said.

Gazprom is also at the forefront of gas use as a transport fuel. Vyakhirev said 200 Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) filling stations in Russia fill 80,000 cars a day, and good results have been obtained experimenting with LNG for rail and river transport as well as in helicopters.

But power generation is a bigger market. "The share of thermal power plants operating on gas is 53 percent in Russia compared with 16 percent in Europe and 15 percent in the U.S.," he said. "Gazprom is aware of the growing role of gas in the Russian economy".
Gazprom has huge political clout. Vyakhirev's predecessor, Viktor Chernomyrdin, is the current prime minister, while Pyotr Rodionov, another former Gazprom man, of minister of fuel and energy.
Asked if Gazprom is now so influential that it actually runs Russia, Vyakhirev pointed out that there are company people in plenty of key positions.

"The first deputy to (President Yeltsin's chief of staff, Anatoly) Chubais is a Gazprom man, and a key central Bank man is also one of ours. Unfortunately we have no one in the armed forces", he joked. "Luckily we have very decent chaps in Gazprom".
Energy minister Rodionov added: "Gazprom's image is improving around the world, so the more Gazprom people there are in government, the more Russia's image will improve".
Vyakhirev had the last word. "We will be happy to supply more ministers if they ask nicely," he said.
